presenceLabel: Wyandot town, raid or hunting area here
presenceNote: Wyandot towns were north of the Ohio (Sandusky River, Detroit). The Kentucky link is raids (1780, 1782) and hunting or travel on the Warriors Path; no Wyandot camp in Kentucky is documented. The start year c.1745 is approximate: the Wyandotte Nation dates the move south from Detroit to “within a few years” of 1701, and Wikipedia gives Upper Sandusky as c.1745. The Kentucky raid story is shown for 1780–1782. The place-name story has no dates.
overlapNote: Shared Ohio country with Delaware (Fort McIntosh 1785 gave the land to both), Shawnee (Wyandot claimed the Shawnee lands west of the Miami in the 1789 Fort Harmar record: 'the Shawanese are only living upon it by their permission'), Mingo and Odawa. In Kentucky the same hunting grounds were used by Shawnee, Delaware, Mingo, Miami (Henderson 1992) and claimed by Shawnee, Cherokee and, by sale, Six Nations.
basis: Treaty text (Fort McIntosh 1785, Greenville 1795), Wyandotte Nation history page, Wikipedia for the 1780/1782 raids, USFS appendix for the name. Town points from Wikipedia coordinates.

wyandot-name-kah-ten-tah-teh-fair-land-o.presenceNote: This story is about a place name, not a territory: it has no dates and no mapped boundary. The Wyandot themselves lived north of the Ohio (Sandusky River, Detroit); their link to Kentucky was hunting and travel on the Warriors Path, and raids in 1780 and 1782 (see the Wyandot raids story).

eras.label: c.1745–1785 · Sandusky and Detroit towns
eras.text: Wyandot (Wendat/Tionontati/Wenro refugees) settled near Detroit from 1701 and sent a branch south to the Sandusky River (Upper Sandusky) in the 1730s-40s. Their towns were north of the Ohio. Detroit and Sandusky points are approximate; the Ohio counties are a general area only.

eras.label: 1780–1782 · Raids on Kentucky stations
eras.text: Wyandot warriors took part in the June 1780 attacks on Ruddle's and Martin's Stations, then in the 15-17 Aug 1782 siege of Bryan Station beside Lenape, Shawnee and Caldwell's Rangers, and in the ambush at Blue Licks on 19 Aug. The points mark events, not Wyandot camps. No Kentucky camp site is documented.

eras.label: 1785 · Fort McIntosh allotment
eras.text: The 21 Jan 1785 Fort McIntosh treaty allotted the lands inside its line to the Wyandot and Delaware "to live and to hunt on", with Ottawa already living there, and made them give up land east, south and west. About one third of Ohio. Only the sourced legs are drawn, dashed, outside Kentucky.

eras.label: 1795 · Greenville
eras.text: At Greenville (3 Aug 1795) the Wyandot, with Delaware, Shawnee, Miami and others, ceded land east and south of the Greenville line. The line ends on the Ohio opposite the mouth of the Kentucky River.

eras.label: Undated · Kah-ten-tah-teh (place name)
eras.text: The U.S. Forest Service history appendix records that Wyandots who often came south of the Ohio to hunt or to travel the Warriors Path called the country Kah-ten-tah-teh, “Fair Land of Tomorrow”. A name is not a territory: this page has no boundary and no dates, and nothing is drawn on the map.

properties.note: Upper Sandusky, Wyandot Co., Ohio (Wikipedia 40.8275, -83.2814). Wyandotte Nation: part of the tribe settled Upper Sandusky after Cadillac's 1701 invitation to Detroit. A BGSU thesis places the 1780s 'Sandusky Old Town' about five miles north of modern Upper Sandusky and moved in April 1782 to Crane Township; point is the modern city, good to a few miles.
